In deploying algorithms, we may be interested in properties beyond just the asymptotic runtime that classical theory focuses on.
This includes an algorithm's non-asymptotic behavior on actually encountered instances, space usage and restrictions imposed by the input model.
Here, we focus on the latter two: algorithms that must interact with a large amounts of data arriving over time without having the memory to store all of it.
This is a common occurence in large data-intesive applications; for example, when aggregating statistics for social media platforms, network traffic or databases.
Many of the algorithms we discuss are powering some of the most substantial systems in the world as we speak! 

## The Model 

Our algorithms must deal with massively long input streams $\sigma$ whose elements are themselves drawn from a massive universe.
The simplest model, dubbed the *vanilla streaming model*, only allows an algorithm to read the stream once. 
We define this model a bit formally to clarify these notions and our notation.

::: {#def-stream}
# Stream
A stream $\sigma$ is a sequence $\langle a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m \rangle$ whose elements, called *tokens*, are drawn from the universe $\mathcal U \defeq [n]$.
:::

Viewing $m, n$ as being quite large, naturally the main goal for us--besides an efficient runtime-- is using little space. 
Particularly, storing the entire stream would take $m \log n$ bits, which we expect to be prohibitively large.
As a result, we want the number of bits $s$ used by our algorithms to be sublinear in both $m, n$. 
That is, we want $s \in o(\min\{m , n\})$. 
We would be quite happy with $s \in O(\polylog(m, n))$ and absolutely ecstatic with $O(\log m + \log n)$-- the same amount of space as storing a constant number of tokens and a constant number of counters.

::: {#def-s-streaming-alg}
# $s$-Space, Single Pass Streaming Algorithm

A *pass* over a stream $\sigma$ consists of reading its tokens once, sequentially from $a_1$ to $a_m$. 

An $s$-space, single pass streaming algorithm makes a single pass over the input stream, using at most $s$ bits of memory at all times.

A randomized algorithm is further allowed to generate fresh, independent, unbiased random bits at any time.
:::

Crucially, during a pass, an algorithm can access earlier tokens in a stream only through what it has saved in its working memory. 
Any random bits retained for later use also count to the memory bound.

We further assume that the machine memory is organized as a collection of *words*, each of which store $\log n$ bits-- this is a natural choice as each token $a_i$ then ccupies a single word of memory. 
Our analysis is also made slightly easier in that we don't have to carry a factor of $\log n$ which appears when counting the number of bits used directly.

In many cases, randomization lets us achieve space guarantees that determinism cannot or at least provides an easier way to do so. 
In that case, we often want an $(\eps, \delta)$-style PAC guarantee from the algorithm: the algorithm's output, with probability $> 1 - \delta$, should approximate the target quantity with relative error $< \epsilon$

Throughout, unless otherwise stated, we stick to the notation established here: that is, $n$ always denotes the stream length; $m$ always denotes the universe size; $a$ and $a_i$ always denote tokens; $s$ denotes the number of bits used by the algorithm considered.
Now, for all the fun!

## Heavy Hitters

We begin by considering the problem of identifying tokens that show up frequently in the stream.

::: {#def-heavy-hitter}
# $k$-Heavy Hitter

Suppose $k \in \N^+$. A $k$-heavy hitter is a value that occurs more than $n/k$ times in the stream.

:::

::: {#prb-heavy-hitters}
# $k$ Heavy Hitters

Given $k \in \N^+$ and a stream, output a set that contains all the $k$-heavy hitters.

:::

Note that the output is allowed to contain elements that aren't $k$-heavy hitters too.

### Boyer-Moore
As a warmup consider the $2$-heavy-hitter problem-- that is, we want to find a token attaining simple majority.

The following is an algorithm due to @boyer1991mjrtyfast.
 
```{.pseudocode #alg-boyer-moore caption="Boyer-Moore"}
\State $x \gets \perp, c \gets 0$
\For{$i \in [m]$}
  \State \textbf{observe} $a_i$
  \If{$c = 0$}
    \State $x \gets a_i$
    \State $c \gets 1$
  \Else
    \State $c \gets c + 2 \cdot \textbf{1} \{a_i = x\} - 1$
  \EndIf
\EndFor

\Output $x$
```


### Misra-Gries
The prior algorithm generalizes to solve the @prb-heavy-hitters problem too as shown by @misra1982findingrepeated.

```{.pseudocode #alg-misra-gries caption="Misra-Gries"}
\State $(x_j, c_j) \gets (\perp, 0)$ for $j \in [k - 1]$
\For{$i \in [m]$}
  \State \textbf{observe} $a_i$
  \If{$c_j = 0$ for some $j \in [k - 1]$}
    \State $x_j \gets a_i$
    \State $c \gets 1$
  \Elif{$a_i = x_j$ for some $j \in [k - 1]$}
    \State $c_j \gets c_j + 1$
  \Else
    \State $c_j \gets c_j - 1$ for all $j \in [k - 1]$
  \EndIf
\EndFor

\Output $x$
```

## Sampling a Multisubset
It is often useful to be able to maintain a representative sample of the stream we are given. 
This also motivates a natural class of algorithms for a variety of problems in the streaming setting: keep track of a representative sample, compute statistics on it and use this to estimate the target statistic for the whole stream.

::: {#prb-sample-multiset}
# Uniform Token Sampling
Given $t \in \N^+$, select a uniform random $t$-element subset $I \subseteq [n]$ and output the multiset of values $[a_i \, \mid \, i \in I]$.
:::

The following is a well-known, widely-applicable way of solving this.

```{.pseudocode #alg-res-sampling caption="Reservoir Sample"}
\State \textbf{given:} $t \in \N^+$
\State $(b_1, \dots, b_t) \gets (\perp, \dots, \perp)$
\For{$i \in [m]$}
  \State \textbf{observe} $a_i$
  \If{$i \le t$}
    \State $b_i \gets a_i$
  \Else 
    \State \textbf{with probability $t/i$:} 
      \State $\hspace{1.2em}$ \textbf{sample} $i \sim \textrm{Uni}([t])$
      \State $\hspace{1.2em}$ $b_i \gets a_i$
  \EndIf
\EndFor
\State\textbf{output} $(b_1, \dots, b_t)$
```

### Rank Estimation

We are interested in computing the "emperical" CDF of the stream.

::: {#def-rank}
# Rank

The rank of a token $a \in \mathcal U$ relative to this stream is
$$
\begin{aligned}
r(a) = \frac{\# \left\{ i \, \mid \, a_i \le a \right\}}{m}.
\end{aligned}
$$

We say that $\hat{r}(a)$ is an $\eps$-approximate rank of $a$ when $\abs{\hat r(a) - r(a)} < \eps$.
:::

::: {#prb-rank}
# Rank Estimation

Given $\eps, \delta > 0$, output, for every fixed $a \in \mathcal U$, an $\eps$-approximate rank of $a$ with probability greater than $1 - \delta$. 
That is, for every $a \in \mathcal U$, output $\hat r(a)$ such that 
$$
\Pr \left\{ \abs{\hat r(a) - r(a)} \ge \eps \right\} \le \delta
$$
:::


We apply reservoir-sampling in the obvious way alluded before,


<!-- \State \textbf{choose some } $t \ge \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon^{-2} \ln(2/\delta)$ -->
```{.pseudocode #alg-rank-est caption="Rank Estimation"}
\State $(b_1, \dots, b_t) \gets \textrm{Reservoir-Sample}(t)$
\State \textbf{define }
  $\hat{r}(a) \coloneqq  \# \left\{ j \in [t] \, \mid \, b_j \le a \right\}/ t $
\State \textbf{output} $\hat q$
```


### Uniform Rank Estimation
It would be desirable that a single $\hat r$ approximates $r$ well for all $a \in \mathcal U$ in the following sense,

::: {#prb-uni-rank}
# Uniform Rank Estimation

Given $\eps, \delta > 0$, output a $\hat r$ satisfying $\norm{\hat r - r}_\infty < \eps$ with probability greater than $1 - \delta$.
:::

By the union bound, if, for each $a \in \mathcal U$, we know that $\hat r (a)$ is an $(\eps, \delta/n)$-PAC for @prb-rank then $\hat r(a)$ is an $(\eps, \delta)$-PAC for @prb-uni-rank. 
Applying this to @alg-rank-est, we would use $t = \Theta \left(\frac{1}{2} \eps^{-2} \ln(2m/\delta)\right)$ samples to solve @prb-uni-rank.

Surprisingly, we can show that @alg-rank-est can solve @prb-uni-rank with just $t \in \Theta \left( 2 \eps^{-2} \ln \left( \frac{4}{\eps \delta} \right) \right)$ samples.

An even sharper analysis using the DKW inequality (see @boudec2026elementaryproof for a simplified proof) shows that @alg-rank-est can in fact solve @prb-uni-rank with $t \in \Theta \left( \frac{1}{2} \eps^{-2} \ln(2/\delta) \right)$!

<!-- Greenwald-Khanna ? -->

## Hapaxes

We are now interested in streaming algorithms for estimating the number of *unique* elements in a stream. 

::: {#def-hapax}
# Hapax
An element that occurs *exactly once* in a stream is called a hapax. 
By $h$ we denote the number of hapaxes in a stream.
:::

::: {#prb-hapax}
# Hapax Estimation
Given $\eps, \delta > 0$, output $\hat h$ such that $\abs{\hat h - h} < \eps \cdot m$ with probability greater than $1 - \delta$.
:::

We will use this problem to showcase a variety of useful techniques!

First on the docket, we present a useful trick for amplifying an $(\eps, 1/3)$-PAC guarantee to a $(\eps, \delta)$-PAC guarantee.

::: {#lem-amplify}
Suppose an algorithm $\mathcal A$ satisfyes a $(\eps, 1/3)$-PAC guarantee for estimating a quantity $x$ then there exists an $(\eps, \delta)$-PAC algorithm for estimating $x$ too.
:::
::: {.proof key=lem-amplify}

Suppose $k$ is odd with $k \ge 18 \eps^2 \ln \frac{1}{\delta}$

Run $k$ independent copies of $\mathcal A$, denoting the resulting estimates $\hat{x}_1, \dots, \hat{x}_k$.

Our estimate will then be $\hat{x} = \text{median}(\hat{x}_1, \dots, \hat{x}_k)$. 
Define 
$X_i \defeq \mathbf 1 \{ \hat{x}_i \notin [(1 - \eps) \cdot x, (1 + \eps) \cdot x] \}$, 
for $i \in [k]$ and $X = \sum X_i$.

We have $\E X_i = 1/3$ and $\E X = \sum \E X_i = k/3$.

By Hoeffding's inequality, we have 
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \Pr \left\{ \hat{x} \notin [(1- \eps) \cdot x, (1 + \eps) \cdot x] \right\} 
    &\le \Pr \left\{ X \ge \frac{k}{2} \right\} \\
    &= \Pr \left\{ X - \E X \ge k/6 \right\} \\
    &\le \exp \left( - \frac{k}{\eps^2 18} \right) \le \delta.
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have our $(\epsilon, \delta)$-PAC guarantee.

:::

### Hashing I: Monitoring a Subset of the Buckets



<!-- \State \textbf{choose} a prime $t \in \left[\frac{12m}{\varepsilon}, \frac{24m}{\varepsilon}\right]$ -->
<!-- \State $r \gets \left\lceil \frac{576}{\varepsilon^3} \right\rceil$ -->
```{.pseudocode #alg-hapax-hash-i caption="Bottom-$r$ Monitoring"}
\State \textbf{draw} $h$ from a $2$-universal family $\mathcal{H}$ of $\mathcal{U} \to \mathbb F_t$ functions
\State $(c_1, \dots, c_r) \gets (0, \dots, 0)$
\For{$i \in [m]$}
  \State \textbf{observe} $a_i$
  \If{$h(a_i) \le r$}
    \State $c_{h(a_i)} \gets c_{h(a_i)} + 1$
  \EndIf
\EndFor
\State \textbf{output} $\# \{j \in [r] \, \mid \, c_j = 1\} \cdot (t / r)$
```

### Hashing II: Monitoring the Preimage of a Bucket


<!-- \State \textbf{choose} a prime $t \in \left[ \frac{m\varepsilon^2}{12} , \frac{m \varepsilon^2}{6} \right]$ -->
<!-- \State $r \gets \left\lceil \frac{32}{\varepsilon^2} \right\rceil$ -->
```{.pseudocode #alg-hapax-hash-ii caption="Single Bucket Monitoring"}
\State \textbf{draw} $h$ from a $2$-universal family $\mathcal{H}$ of $\mathcal{U} \to \mathbb F_t$ functions
\State $(b_j, c_j) \gets (\perp, 0)$ for $j \in [r]$
\For{$i \in [m]$}
  \State \textbf{observe} $a_i$
  \If{$h(a_i) = 0$}
  \If{there is $j \in [r]$ with $b_j = a_i$}
    \State $c_j \gets c_j + 1$
  \ElseIf{there is $j \in [r]$ with $b_j = \perp$}
    \State $b_j \gets a_i$
    \State $c_j \gets 1$
  \EndIf
  \EndIf
\EndFor
\State \textbf{observe} $\# \{ j \in [r] \, \mid \, c_j = 1 \} \cdot t$
```

### Reservoir Sampling

<!-- \State \textbf{choose} $t \ge \frac{2 \ln 6}{\varepsilon^2}$ -->
```{.pseudocode #alg-hapax-res caption="Reservoir Sampling for Hapax"}
\State \textbf{sample} a random $t$-subset $\{ j_1 < \dots < j_t \} \subseteq [n]$ using reservoir sampling
\State \textbf{maintain} counters $j \in [t]$,
\State $\hspace{1.2em} c_j \gets$ number of instances of token $a_{j_k}$ after position $j_k$ (inclusive)
\State \textbf{output} $\# \{ j \in [t] \, \mid \, c_j = 1 \} - \# \{ j \in [t] \, \mid \, c_j = 2 \}$
```


## $F_2$ Estimation

::: {#def-f-k}
By $\vec f \in \N^{\, \mathcal U}$ denote the frequency vector; that is, $f_a$ denotes the frequency of $a$ in the given stream for each $a \in \mathcal U$.
We define the $F_k$ statistic as
$$
\begin{aligned}
    F_k \defeq \sum_{a \in \mathcal U} f_i^k = \norm{\vec f}_k^k.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

The following is the Tug-of-War sketch from the seminal work of @alonspacecomplexity.
```{.pseudocode #alg-f-2 caption="$F_2$ estimation"}
\State \textbf{draw} $h$ from a $4$-universal family $\mathcal{H}$ of $\mathcal{U} \to \{-1, + 1\}$ functions
\State $c \gets 0$
\For{$i \in [m]$}
  \State \textbf{observe} $a_i$
  \State $c \gets c + h(a_i)$
\EndFor
\State \textbf{output} $c^2$
```


## Distinct Elements

We wish to estimate the cardinality of the stream-- in other words, the number of distinct elements. 
Throughout this section we use $m_d$ to denote the number of distinct elelemts.

::: {#prb-distinct-els}
# Cardinality Estimation

Given $\eps, \delta > 0$, output $\hat{m}_d$ such that $\abs{\hat{m}_d - m_d} < \eps$ with probability greater than $1 - \delta$.
:::

### Flajolet-Martin

As a warmup to illustrate some crucial ideas, we focus on a weaker version that only requires a multiplicative guarantee.

::: {#prb-distinct-els}
# Multiplicattive Cardinality Estimation

Given $\eps > 0$, output $\hat{m}_d$ such that $\hat{m}_d \in \left[ \frac{m_d}{6}, 6 \cdot m_d \right]$ with probability greater than $1 - \delta$.
:::

The following is a reframing of an algorithm from @flajolet1985probabilisticcounting by @bar-yossef2002countingdistinct.


```{.pseudocode #alg-fm caption="Flajolet-Martin"}
\State \textbf{draw} $h$ from a $2$-universal family $\mathcal{H}$ of $\mathcal{U} \to \mathbb{F}_t$ functions
\State $Z \gets \min \{ h(a_i) \, \mid \, i \in [m]\}$
\State \textbf{output} $t/Z$
```

### Bottom-$r$ Sketch

We use ideas similar to @alg-hapax-hash-i: that is, look at the earliest $r$ buckets that are hashed to and use this to estimate the number of distinct elements.

## Frequency Estimation

Now, we shift from estimating some statistic $g(\vec f)$ of the frequency vector $\vec f$ to estimating $\vec f$ itself.

### Count-Min Sketch

::: {#prb-f-2-est}
# Additive $\vec f$ Estimation
Give $\eps, \delta > 0$, output $\vec c$ such that, for each token $a$, in the stream $\abs{c_a - f_a} < \eps m$ with probability greater than $1 - \delta$.
:::

```{.pseudocode #alg-count-min caption="Count-Min Sketch"}

```

### Count Sketch

::: {#prb-f-2-est}
# Relative $\vec f$ Estimation
Give $\eps, \delta > 0$, output $\hat c$ such that, for each token $a$, in the stream $\abs{c_a - f_a} < \eps \norm{\vec f}_2$ with probability greater than $1 - \delta$.
:::
